title: fix: OIDC expiry 0 sets nil instead of far-future date
body:
Fixes #3111

## Problem

When `oidc.expiry` is set to `0` (meaning "no expiry"), headscale sets the node expiry to `MaxDuration` (~292 years in the future). This results in a far-future date like `2318-06-08` in the database instead of NULL. Clients like Headplane cannot distinguish this from a real expiry and fail to show the "no expiry" tag.

## Fix

Three changes:

1. **`hscontrol/oidc.go` - `determineNodeExpiry`**: When `Expiry` equals `MaxDuration`, return zero time instead of adding 292 years to now.

2. **`hscontrol/oidc.go` - `handleRegistration`**: When the computed expiry is zero time, pass `nil` (instead of `&expiry`) to `HandleNodeFromAuthPath`, resulting in NULL in the database. This is consistent with how `IsExpired()` already treats nil expiry as "not expired".

3. **`hscontrol/types/config.go`**: Exported `MaxDuration` so it can be referenced from the `hscontrol` package.

## Test

Added `TestDetermineNodeExpiry` with three test cases:
- `zero_expiry_means_no_expiry`: verifies MaxDuration config returns zero time (fails without fix: returns year 2318)
- `normal_expiry_returns_future_time`: verifies normal expiry still works
- `use_token_expiry`: verifies UseExpiryFromToken still works

Tested locally on macOS ARM (Apple Silicon). All hscontrol tests pass.

title: policy: add App Connector support via nodeAttrs
body:
App connector configuration is now delivered through the `nodeAttrs` `app` field, the way Tailscale delivers it, instead of the custom `appConnectors` policy block this PR originally added. Rebased on current main.

Following up on @Matchlighter's suggestion: after #3251 landed nodeAttrs, the only missing piece was valued capabilities. `nodeAttrs` carried key-only caps through `attr` and nothing else.

## What changed

1. `NodeAttrGrant` gets an `app` field (`tailcfg.NodeCapMap`), stamped into the node's CapMap in `compileNodeAttrs` next to the key-only attrs. Payloads are passed through opaquely and the client interprets them.
2. App connectors ride that generic path, so there is no app-connector-specific code left anywhere: `compileNodeAttrs` -> `NodeCapMap` -> `NodesWithChangedCapMap` -> `SelfUpdate`.
3. The `PolicyChange{IncludeSelf: true}` broadcast the first version needed is gone. A reload now sends a targeted self update only to nodes whose config actually changed, which also fixes the reload propagation @dmeremyanin hit.
4. Removed: the `appConnectors` block, the `AppConnector` / `AppConnectorAttr` types, `AppConnectorConfigForNode` and its wrappers, the `builder.go` injection, and the load-time domain validation.

```json
{
  "tagOwners": {
    "tag:connector": ["admin@"]
  },
  "nodeAttrs": [
    {
      "target": ["tag:connector"],
      "app": {
        "tailscale.com/app-connectors": [
          {
            "name": "Internal Apps",
            "connectors": ["tag:connector"],
            "domains": ["internal.example.com", "*.corp.example.com"],
            "routes": ["10.0.0.0/8"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## What works and what does not

Works today: the capability reaches every node the `target` selects, hardcoded `routes` are advertised as soon as the connector gets its config, and policy reloads propagate.

Does not work yet: Headscale does not tell clients to send DNS queries for the configured domains to the connector, so dynamic domain discovery does not happen on its own. That is the DNS side of the feature and it belongs with the v0.31 work. `docs/ref/policy.md` says so in a warning admonition, `features.md` marks App Connectors unchecked with the delivery part checked underneath, so nobody reads this as done.

Two deliberate behavior notes:

1. The cap ships on `target` match regardless of `tailscale set --advertise-connector`. This matches Tailscale, where the client gates on its local connector flag and on the payload's `connectors` field.
2. No load-time domain validation. Payloads are pass through, so a malformed domain surfaces client side.

## Cap name validation

Grant `app` cap names go through `validateCapabilityName`, which rejects URL-formatted names and `tailscale.com/*` names that are not in `tailscaleCapAllowlist`. The `app` field on nodeAttrs needs the same guard, otherwise a policy can ship any `tailscale.com` capability to a node with nothing behind it:

```json
{ "target": ["*"], "app": { "tailscale.com/cap/funnel": [] } }
```

So there is a `validateNodeCapabilityName` with its own allowlist, currently holding only `tailscale.com/app-connectors`. It is a separate map because `tailscaleCapAllowlist` is keyed by `tailcfg.PeerCapability` and its comment is about peer caps. Names in an operator's own domain, like `example.com/app/my-cap`, still pass through. The reasoning is the one already in `nodeAttrUnsupportedCaps`: rejecting at load beats letting a node advertise something that does not work.

If you would rather have one shared allowlist, or no gate at all on the nodeAttrs side, say so and I will change it.

## Tests

Unit (`hscontrol/policy/v2/appconnector_test.go`), on the shared nodeAttrs fixtures:

1. `TestAppConnectorViaNodeAttrs`: targeted node gets both configs, non-targeted nodes get nothing, `routes` round trips through `appctype.AppConnectorAttr`.
2. `TestAppConnectorWildcardTarget`: `*` reaches every node.
3. `TestAppConnectorChangeTracking`: the cap participates in `NodesWithChangedCapMap`, which is what makes the `IncludeSelf` removal safe.
4. `TestValidateNodeCapabilityName` and `TestAppConnectorUnsupportedCapRejected`: the allowlist, both at the helper and at policy load.

Integration (`integration/appconnector_test.go`): `TestAppConnectorBasic`, `TestAppConnectorNonMatchingTag`, `TestAppConnectorWildcardConnector`. Configs are marshalled through `appctype.AppConnectorAttr` so the tests use the same wire shape a Tailscale hosted control plane emits.

title: Tracking: Flaky integration and unit tests
body:
Tracking issue for flaky tests identified by systematically analyzing CI results across ~75 merged PRs.

Supersedes #2299 and #2935.

## Flaky Tests

Failure rate is approximate, based on ~40 PRs that ran integration tests.

### Critical (~20-42% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestAutoApproveMultiNetwork` (all subtests) — `integration/route_test.go:2037` — ~42% failure rate. ACL/route auto-approve changes don't propagate within EventuallyWithT timeouts on CI runners.
- [ ] `TestACLTagPropagation` — `integration/acl_test.go:2296` — ~20% failure rate. Tag change propagation too slow for CI. Subtests `multiple-tags-partial-removal` and `remove-tag-revokes-access` are worst offenders.

### High (~7-12% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific` — `integration/acl_test.go:2852` — ~12%. Port-specific ACL changes via tags don't propagate in time.
- [ ] `TestACLHostsInNetMapTable` — `integration/acl_test.go:101` — ~7%. ACL propagation timing.
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIPManyUpDown` — `integration/general_test.go:1391` — ~7%. Ping failures during up/down cycling.

### Medium (~5% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestAuthWebFlowAuthenticationPingAll` — `integration/auth_web_flow_test.go:18`
- [ ] `TestOIDCExpiryAfterRestart` — `integration/auth_oidc_test.go:1352`
- [ ] `TestEphemeral2006DeletedTooQuickly` — `integration/general_test.go:213`

### Low (~2% failure rate)

- [ ] `TestNodeOnlineStatus` — `integration/general_test.go:1266`
- [ ] `TestAuthWebFlowLogoutAndReloginSameUser` — `integration/auth_web_flow_test.go:60`
- [ ] `TestTagsUserLoginReauthWithEmptyTagsRemovesAllTags` — `integration/tags_test.go:2827`
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIP` — `integration/general_test.go:28`
- [ ] `TestPingAllByIPPublicDERP` — `integration/general_test.go:90`
- [ ] `TestSSHAutogroupSelf` — `integration/ssh_test.go:546`
- [ ] `TestEphemeralInAlternateTimezone` — `integration/general_test.go:131`
- [ ] `TestSubnetRouteACLFiltering` — `integration/route_test.go:2952`

### Unit tests

- [ ] `TestBatcherScalabilityAllToAll` — `hscontrol/mapper/batcher_test.go:580` — Panic: send on closed channel. Race condition in LockFreeBatcher shutdown.
- [ ] `TestAuthenticationFlows` — `hscontrol/auth_test.go:38` — Intermittent 401 from registration cache expiration. (#2935)
- [ ] `TestOIDC024UserCreation` — `integration/auth_oidc_test.go:238` — Non-deterministic DB row ordering. (#2299)

## Common root causes

1. **ACL/tag propagation timing** — Most flakes. EventuallyWithT timeouts too short for CI runners.
2. **Network connectivity races** — Ping timeouts under CI load.
3. **Client startup timeouts** — Tailscale clients don't reach Running state within 2min on slow CI.
4. **Go race conditions** — Actual code bugs (LockFreeBatcher, registration cache).

title: integration: reduce flaky test failures on CI
body:
Reduce flakiness in integration tests that fail on CI due to resource-constrained runners.

- Scale EventuallyWithT timeouts using PeerSyncTimeout (60s local, 120s CI)
- Use CurlFailFast for assertions expecting connection failure
- Use relaxed ping settings (2s timeout, DERP acceptable) instead of defaults (200ms, direct-only)
- Increase polling intervals for expensive operations (curl, traceroute)

title: [Bug] Newly connected nodes cannot use subnet routers after a netmap stream flap
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

After a transient connection issue affecting a subnet router, Headscale logs warnings like
```json
{"level":"warn","error":"connection 10b0c6925e5a6b8f: timeout sending to channel (likely stale connection)","node.id":122,"chan":"0x182ad4e013b0","conn.id":"10b0c6925e5a6b8f","connection_index":0,"time":1772763603,"message":"send: connection send failed"}
```

Node 122 is the subnet router.

From that point on, nodes that connect **after the event** cannot use that subnet router. Existing nodes that already knew about the router continue to work normally. The problem persists until the subnet router reconnects or Headscale is restarted.

In addition, restarting Headscale does not exit cleanly in this state: **the process hangs during shutdown** and only terminates if killed with SIGKILL.

### Expected Behavior

A temporary network flap or broken netmap stream should not leave a subnet router in a permanently degraded state. Newly connected nodes should be able to use the subnet router without requiring a Headscale restart or a router reconnect.

Headscale should also shut down cleanly instead of hanging during restart.

### Steps To Reproduce

I don't have a fully deterministic reproducer, but the issue appears with this pattern:
1. Run Headscale with at least one subnet router advertising approved routes.
2. Ensure existing clients can reach the routed subnet through that router.
3. Trigger a transient connection problem affecting the subnet router's netmap stream.
4. Observe Headscale log warnings like: `timeout sending to channel (likely stale connection)`.
5. Connect a new node to the tailnet after that event.
6. Observe that the new node cannot use the subnet router, while older nodes still can.
7. Reconnect the subnet router or restart Headscale.
8. Observe that newly connected nodes start working through the subnet router again.
9. In the restart case, observe that Headscale may hang during shutdown and require SIGKILL.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Ubunut 24.04
- Headscale version: 0.28.0
- Tailscale version: 1.94.2
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Subnet router logs:
```
magicsock: disco: ignoring CallMeMaybe from d:39944a37b731e697; [GL3bW] is unknown
magicsock: disco: ignoring CallMeMaybe from d:8aed5a55372b8ddd; [+tCFc] is unknown
```

--

Based on local debugging, the issue appears to be caused by two pieces of state getting out of sync:
- Headscale still considers the subnet router online and serving routes.
- The live netmap delivery path from Headscale to that router is no longer usable.

Observed sequence:

1. The subnet router's long-poll / netmap session flaps and stops draining updates from its session channel.
2. Headscale attempts to send an update to that router, the enqueue times out in `connectionEntry.send`, and the failed channel is removed in `multiChannelNodeConn.send`.
3. The router entry remains in the batcher for rapid reconnection, and the router remains online in state until the old `mapSession` fully unwinds through `serveLongPoll`.
4. If that old session is stuck in `writeMap()` / `Flush()` while writing to the client, the deferred cleanup in `serveLongPoll` does not run promptly, so the router is not disconnected in state.
5. New nodes connect and their peer updates are queued and broadcast as usual.
6. Those updates are still targeted at the subnet router, but the router no longer has a usable live map channel, so it never receives the new peer information.
7. Existing nodes continue to work because the router already knew about them before the flap.
8. Nodes that connect after the event cannot use the subnet router because the router never learns about those new peers.

This also appears related to the shutdown hang: when the old `mapSession` gets stuck in `writeMap()` / `Flush()`, Headscale can block during shutdown waiting for that client stream to exit.

title: Fix stale netmap sessions after broken client writes
body:
This fixes the case where newly connected nodes can no longer use a subnet router after a flap, and also prevents shutdown from hanging on a stuck netmap stream.

Changes:
- handle `RemoveNode` correctly when the channel was already removed earlier by stale-connection cleanup
- tear down stale map sessions when stale-send cleanup removes a timed-out connection

body:
Closes #3055
Closes #3062

## Summary

- Adds a reusable `warnBanner()` function that prints a large ASCII-art "Warning!" banner to the log output, matching the format from #3055
- Modifies `prefixV4()` and `prefixV6()` to return a boolean indicating whether the configured prefix is outside the standard range, instead of logging independently
- Consolidates the check in `LoadServerConfig()` so the banner fires **once** even if both prefixes are non-standard
- Updates `config-example.yaml` to clarify that subsets of the default ranges are fine, but ranges outside CGNAT/ULA are not

## What the warning looks like

When a user configures a prefix outside the standard CGNAT or ULA range, they'll see something like this at startup:

```

###                                                          ###
###  You have overridden the default Headscale IP prefixes   ###
###  with a range outside of the standard CGNAT and/or ULA   ###
###  ranges. This is NOT a supported configuration.          ###
```

title: fix: persist empty ApprovedRoutes and Endpoints to database
body:
## Summary

Fixes #3110

When an admin rejects all routes for a node (`headscale nodes approve-routes -i 5 -r ""`), the empty `ApprovedRoutes` slice is correctly set in the in-memory NodeStore but never written to the database. On restart, the old routes reappear.

**Root cause**: `persistNodeToDB` uses GORM's `.Updates(struct)`, which silently skips zero-value fields. An empty `[]netip.Prefix` is a zero value, so it's dropped.

**Fix**: After the `.Updates()` call in `persistNodeToDB`, explicitly persist empty `ApprovedRoutes` and `Endpoints` slices by writing `"[]"` — the same pattern already used in `db.SetApprovedRoutes` (node.go:242-244).

This is done in `persistNodeToDB` rather than individual callers so it fixes the issue for all code paths, and also addresses a latent bug where `Endpoints` could similarly fail to persist when empty.

title: [Feature] Add stun_only mode for embedded DERP server
body:
### Use case

Headscale's embedded DERP server currently always runs in full mode (STUN + DERP relay). While this works for most users, some have specific needs to only provide STUN service without relaying traffic.

Specific scenarios:
1. Bandwidth-constrained deployments: Users with limited egress bandwidth (cloud VPS with traffic caps, metered connections) want to avoid the cost of relaying traffic while still assisting with NAT traversal
2. Hybrid infrastructure: Prefer using local Headscale for STUN (fast discovery) + Tailscale's global DERP network for actual relay (better distributed infrastructure)
3. Compliance/privacy requirements: Some organizations prefer not to handle relay traffic on their own infrastructure

Default behavior unchanged: This feature would be opt-in only (stun_only: false by default), ensuring no impact on existing deployments.

### Description

Currently, when derp.server.enabled: true, Headscale:
• Starts STUN service on UDP 3478
• Starts DERP HTTP service for traffic relay
• Advertises STUNOnly: false to clients
There is no way to disable the relay functionality while keeping STUN.

Proposed solution:
Add optional derp.server.stun_only configuration property:
• When not specified or false (default): Current behavior unchanged - full DERP server with STUN + relay
• When true: Only STUN service starts, no HTTP DERP relay, advertises STUNOnly: true

Usage Example

```
derp:
  server:
    enabled: true
    stun_only: true              # Optional: Enable STUN-only mode (default: false)
    stun_listen_addr: "0.0.0.0:3478"
    region_id: 999
    region_code: "headscale"
    region_name: "Headscale STUN Only"
```

title: Audit and standardize integration test infrastructure options (tsic/hsic)
body:
## Problem

Integration test infrastructure options (`tsic.With*` / `hsic.With*`) are inconsistent across test files, with no documentation explaining *why* specific tests deviate from the common patterns. This has already caused a real bug: `TestACLPolicyPropagationOverTime` was missing `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()`, `WithTLS()`, and `WithNetfilter("off")` — options that every other ACL test uses — causing flaky failures on the `unstable` Tailscale client.

## Specific inconsistencies found

### 1. SSH tests never use embedded DERP

`sshScenario()` (10 tests) skips `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()` and `WithTLS()`, relying on public DERP relays from Docker containers. Potential flakiness vector.

### 2. All 30+ tags tests skip embedded DERP

Every test in `tags_test.go` uses `WithTLS()` but not `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()`. Consistent within the file, but undocumented why.

### 3. `WithDERPAsIP()` without `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()`

5 auth tests use `WithDERPAsIP()` without embedded DERP, which seems meaningless since `WithDERPAsIP()` configures how the embedded DERP advertises itself.

Tests: `TestAuthWebFlowLogoutAndReloginSameUser`, `TestAuthWebFlowLogoutAndReloginNewUser`, `TestAuthKeyLogoutAndReloginNewUser`, `TestAuthKeyDeleteKey`, `TestAuthKeyLogoutAndReloginSameUserExpiredKey` (non-HTTPS mode).

### 4. `TestACLHostsInNetMapTable` is the most minimal ACL test

No `WithTestName`, no `WithTLS()`, no `WithNetfilter("off")`, no embedded DERP. Significantly deviates from every other ACL test.

### 5. `TestPolicyUpdateWhileRunningWithCLIInDatabase` missing embedded DERP

An ACL-related test in `acl_test.go` that skips `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()` and `WithTLS()` despite testing policy propagation with curl.

### 6. Two tests still use custom Docker entrypoints

`TestACLTagPropagation` and `TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific` use inline `apk add` + `python3 -m http.server` in their entrypoint instead of `WithPackages()` + `WithWebserver()`. This is the old pattern that was cleaned up everywhere else in 21ba197d.

### 7. `WithTestName` values reused across unrelated tests

For example, `"clienableroute"` is used by 6 different route tests, `"pingallbyip"` is shared between general and auth key tests. Not a correctness issue (run IDs provide isolation), but makes log analysis harder.

## Proposed work

- [ ] For each test, document (via code comment or a reference table) *why* it uses or omits each infrastructure option
- [ ] Migrate `TestACLTagPropagation` and `TestACLTagPropagationPortSpecific` from custom entrypoints to `WithPackages()` + `WithWebserver()`
- [ ] Evaluate whether SSH tests and tags tests should use embedded DERP (and document if intentionally omitted)
- [ ] Fix `WithDERPAsIP()` without `WithEmbeddedDERPServerOnly()` — either add embedded DERP or remove the meaningless option
- [ ] Evaluate `TestACLHostsInNetMapTable` and `TestPolicyUpdateWhileRunningWithCLIInDatabase` for missing options
- [ ] Deduplicate `WithTestName` values across unrelated tests

title: Serialize per-node work to prevent out-of-order delivery
body:
`processBatchedChanges` queues each pending change for a node as a separate work item. Since multiple workers pull from the same channel, two changes for the same node can be processed concurrently by different workers. This causes two problems:

1. MapResponses can be delivered out of order — a later change might finish generating before an earlier one, so the client sees stale state.
2. `updateSentPeers` and `computePeerDiff` race against each other — `updateSentPeers` does `Clear()` + `Store()` which isn't atomic relative to a concurrent `Range` in `computePeerDiff`.

The fix is either merging all pending changes for a node into a single work item before queuing (so each node gets at most one work item per batch tick), or using worker affinity so a given nodeID always routes to the same worker. Merging is probably simpler and also eliminates redundant MapResponse generation — right now if a node has 5 pending changes, we generate 5 separate MapResponses when one would suffice.

title: Simplify the connected map's three-state encoding
body:
The `b.connected` map uses `*time.Time` to encode three states:
- `nil` value → node is connected
- non-nil `*time.Time` → node disconnected at that timestamp
- key missing → node was never seen

This is easy to get wrong and hard to reason about. The `b.nodes` map combined with `hasActiveConnections()` already provides a reliable source of truth for whether a node is connected right now. We should evaluate whether `b.connected` can be removed entirely, or at minimum replaced with a clearer type (e.g. a struct with an explicit state enum). The disconnect timestamp is only consumed by `cleanupOfflineNodes`, which could alternatively check the node's `lastUsed` timestamp or track disconnection time directly on the `multiChannelNodeConn`.

title: [Feature] Do not crash on unavailable DERPMap URL

### Use case

At present, if one of the URLs provided to `derp.urls` is unavailable (i.e. server down for maintenance, incorrect configuration resulting in 404's, etc), headscale will crash and refuse to start. Unlike loading maps from the local filesystem, which the headscale owner can be fully expected to control, the servers on the other side of those URLs may be controlled by a third party, so crashing or requiring manual intervention in that case is not reasonable.

### Description

Add a new boolean configuration field `derp.allow_unavailable_urls` which defaults to false, and if true,  `derp.urls` that are unavailable or return invalid results will result in a logged warning instead of a crash.

title: mapper/batcher: replace connected map with per-node disconnectedAt
body:
The Batcher's connected field used *time.Time pointer semantics to encode three states: nil meant connected, non-nil meant disconnected-at-timestamp, and key-missing meant never-seen. This was easy to misread (nil meaning "connected" inverts typical Go idioms), redundant with the nodes map that already tracks active connections, and required keeping two parallel concurrent maps in sync. It also contained a bug where RemoveNode used new(time.Now()) instead of &now, producing a zero-valued timestamp.

This replaces the separate connected map with a disconnectedAt atomic.Pointer[time.Time] field directly on multiChannelNodeConn, the object that already manages each node's connections. IsConnected drops from two map lookups to one, ConnectedMap and Debug iterate a single map instead of two, and cleanupOfflineNodes scans b.nodes directly. The markDisconnectedIfNoConns helper is removed.

body:
processBatchedChanges queued each pending change for a node as a separate work item. Since multiple workers pull from the same channel, two changes for the same node could be processed concurrently by different workers. This caused out-of-order MapResponse delivery and a data race between updateSentPeers (Clear+Store) and computePeerDiff (Range) on the shared lastSentPeers map.

This change bundles all pending changes for a node into a single work item so one worker processes them sequentially. ## Summary

Regarding Headscale logs this is what the AI summarized for me:

1. Batcher Atomicity: Under high load, Headscale pushes endpoint updates for NodeKeys that are not yet present in the client's peer list, causing Tailscale clients to fail with IPC error -22 and shut down their UAPI pipe.
2. Database Inconsistency: Bursts of node not found (404) errors occur during the OIDC login flow, resulting in clients receiving peer maps with 0 peers.
3. JSON Truncation: Periodic unexpected end of JSON input errors (500) suggest the MapResponse generator is hitting a concurrency or buffer limit when handling large numbers of nodes.
4. Infrastructure context: Issue observed on a setup using SQLite on DRBD with ~230 nodes and Keycloak OIDC.

User can re-connect to the Tailscale server(s) with no issues.

title: [Bug] DestroyUser deletes ALL pre-auth keys in the database, not just the target user's key
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

When deleting a user via `DELETE /api/v1/user/{id}`, **all pre-auth keys in the entire system are deleted**, not just the keys belonging to the deleted user. This affects every user's keys, making it impossible for any user to register new devices.

For example: if there are 3 users (A, B, C) each with a pre-auth key, deleting user C results in 0 keys remaining — users A and B lose their keys too.

### Expected Behavior

Only the pre-auth keys belonging to the deleted user should be removed. Other users' keys should remain intact.

### Steps To Reproduce

```bash
# 1. Create two users
headscale users create userA
headscale users create userB

# 2. Create a pre-auth key for each (use numeric user IDs from 'headscale users list')
headscale preauthkeys create --user <userA_id> --reusable --expiration 720h
headscale preauthkeys create --user <userB_id> --reusable --expiration 720h

# 3. Verify both keys exist
headscale preauthkeys list
# Shows 2 keys

# 4. Delete userB (must have no nodes)
headscale users delete --identifier <userB_id> --force

# 5. Check keys again
headscale preauthkeys list
# Shows 0 keys — userA's key is also gone
```

Also reproducible via REST API:
```bash
# Verify keys before
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/preauthkey
# Returns 2 keys

# Delete userB
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/user/<userB_id>

# Verify keys after
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/preauthkey
# Returns 0 keys
```

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (Docker host)
- Headscale version: 0.28.0
- Tailscale version: 1.92.4
- Database: SQLite
- Policy mode: database (also tested — the bug exists regardless of policy mode)
- Number of nodes: ~80 across 2 servers
- Runtime: Docker container (`headscale/headscale:0.28.0`)
- Reverse proxy: Caddy 2 (network_mode: host)
- Network: 3 exit nodes (NURO/AMIYA/ARTERIA), 1 subnet router, ~30 users
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

The `pre_auth_keys` table has the correct foreign key constraint:

```sql
CONSTRAINT `fk_pre_auth_keys_user` FOREIGN KEY (`user_id`)
REFERENCES `users`(`id`) ON DELETE SET NULL
```

However, `DestroyUser` explicitly calls `DestroyPreAuthKey` on every key before the user row is deleted, bypassing the `ON DELETE SET NULL` behavior entirely.

### Call chain

```
DELETE /api/v1/user/{id}
  → HeadscaleService_DeleteUser (grpcv1.go)
    → State.DeleteUser (state/state.go)
      → HSDatabase.DestroyUser (db/users.go)
        → ListPreAuthKeys(tx)          ← returns ALL keys
        → DestroyPreAuthKey(tx, key.ID) ← deletes each one
```

### Impact

- **Destructive:** Deleting any single user wipes all pre-auth keys for the entire system
- **Silent:** No error is returned — the API responds 200 OK
- **Data loss:** Keys cannot be recovered without a database backup
- **Connected devices unaffected:** Existing node connections use node keys, not pre-auth keys
- **New registrations blocked:** No user can register new devices until keys are recreated

title: Performance optimizations to handle thousands of clients
body:
- [x] have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) file
- [ ] raised a GitHub issue or discussed it on the projects chat beforehand
- [x] added unit tests
- [ ] added integration tests
- [ ] updated documentation if needed
- [ ] updated CHANGELOG.md

I am part of a CTF organization team that used Headscale and Tailscale to provide a VPN to thousands of participants.
As it is, the current version of Headscale cannot handle it, primarily due to the O(N^2) reachability computation of each node to each node.

I started by replacing the reachability system by a category system, using permission buckets instead of reachability computation. While this was way faster, it also changed over 2000 lines of code, and ripped out a good chunk of existing code.
It has been tested in production and did not seem to have any issues with reachability in any way.

I grabbed my existing changes, pprof, a fresh copy of the repo, and got Claude to gradually, slowly, improve the performance of Headscale until it would be sufficient for our purposes, without changing too much of the existing code.

What is in this PR is the result of this gradual improvement. It is mostly AI generated, and likely contains things that you would not want copied in. See this PR as more of an idea of what could be changed, then.

Anything below this point was AI generated.

---

# perf: registration and policy evaluation optimizations

## Context

This work was done overnight with Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant) running iterative profiling, optimization, and correctness verification cycles against a headscale instance under realistic load.

The goal was to make node registration fast at scale and eliminate idle CPU waste. The benchmark used a brutal ACL policy (500+ tags, 200+ groups, 14K+ filter rules) with thousands of concurrent nodes to surface real bottlenecks.

## Results

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------|-------|
| Registration throughput (2000 nodes, 14.6K rules) | 13/s | 206/s (**15.8x**) |
| Registration throughput (5000 nodes, 14.6K rules) | untested | 77/s avg |
| Idle CPU (2000 nodes connected) | ~70% | **0.85%** |
| Memory (5000 nodes) | - | 872MB |

Correctness was verified at every step:
- All `go test ./hscontrol/...` pass at every commit individually
- 104/104 reachability tests pass (50-container live ACL test with 10 users, 8 roles, 22 rules)
- 149/149 mega-test assertions pass

## Commits (incremental, each builds and passes tests independently)

### 1. `b7ffe48b` hscontrol/policy: defer filter compilation in SetNodes
**4 files, +182/-41**

Moves `compileFilterRules` out of the SetNodes hot path. Instead of recompiling the full filter on every node addition, SetNodes marks the filter dirty and compilation happens lazily on the next `Filter()` or `FilterForNode()` call. This eliminates redundant recompilation when nodes are added in rapid succession (e.g., batch registration).

**Files:** `policy.go` (filterDirty flag, lazy ensureFilterCompiled), `pm.go` (interface update), `state.go` (caller update), `policy_test.go` (new tests for deferred compilation)

### 2. `fcd7a6d7` hscontrol/state,policy: add incremental peer map computation for new node additions
**6 files, +738/-20**

Instead of rebuilding the entire O(N^2) peer map when a new node registers, this adds incremental peer map updates that only compute peers for newly added nodes (O(K*N) where K = new nodes). Includes `RefreshPeersForNodes` which fixes a correctness bug where `PutNode` ran before `SetNodes`, causing stale policy data in peer computation. Also adds `HasPolicyChange` detection for `SubnetRoutes` and `IsExitNode` changes.

**Files:** `node_store.go` (incrementalSnapshot, refreshNodePeers, RefreshPeersForNodes), `policy.go` (SetNodes returns newNodeIDs, HasPolicyChange route detection), `pm.go`, `state.go`, `policy_test.go`, `node_store_test.go`

### 3. `5370bdf9` hscontrol/policy: skip O(N) node iteration in Host.Resolve for non-CGNAT prefixes
**2 files, +77/-12**

`Host.Resolve` was iterating all N nodes for every host entry to check for CGNAT overlap. Since most ACL hosts entries reference external IPs (not CGNAT `100.64.0.0/10` or ULA `fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48`), this adds a fast-path `prefixOverlapsCGNAT` check that skips the node scan entirely for non-overlapping prefixes.

**Files:** `types.go` (prefixOverlapsCGNAT, Resolve fast path), `policy_test.go` (TestHostResolveCGNATSkip)

### 4. `247dbd1b` hscontrol/policy: add source matcher index cache for O(relevant) CanAccess checks
**2 files, +147/-2**

`CanAccess` was iterating all matchers for every source node. This adds `getSrcMatcherIndices` which pre-computes, per source node, which matcher indices have that node's IPs in their source set. Subsequent `CanAccess` calls only check relevant matchers instead of all N matchers.

**Files:** `policy.go` (srcMatcherCache, getSrcMatcherIndices, canAccessIndexed), `policy_test.go` (TestSourceMatcherIndexCache)

### 5. `b1dafc92` hscontrol/policy: hoist invariant checks out of canAccessIndexed inner loop
**1 file, +6/-2**

Moves `len(m.DstIPs)` and `m.IPProto` checks out of the per-destination-IP inner loop in `canAccessIndexed`, since these values don't change per iteration.

**Files:** `policy.go`

### 6. `703960aa` hscontrol/policy: add resolve cache, lightweight filter recompilation, and reachability tests
**4 files, +2616/-7**

Adds a per-compilation-cycle resolve cache for `Group.Resolve`, `Username.Resolve`, and `Tag.Resolve`. The same group/username/tag is referenced hundreds of times across 14K+ ACL rules but resolves identically within one update cycle. The cache achieves ~94% hit rate. Also makes `ensureFilterCompiled` lightweight — it only recompiles filter rules and matchers, skipping redundant tagOwner/autoApprover resolution that `SetNodes` already performed eagerly.

Includes comprehensive reachability test suite: equivalence tests, scale tests, dynamic join/leave, tag changes, subnet route overlap, peer symmetry, connection scenarios, and IP-based ACL rule tests (direct IPs, CIDR ranges, hosts entries, mixed identity+IP rules, IPv6).

**Files:** `policy.go` (resolveCache, lightweight ensureFilterCompiled), `types.go` (cache integration in Resolve methods), `reachability_test.go` (2200+ lines of reachability tests), `reachability_ip_test.go` (IP-based ACL tests)

### 7. `b11db02a` hscontrol/state: replace 500ms batch timeout with 1ms micro-batch drain
**1 file, +108/-29**

The NodeStore batched operations with a 500ms timeout, causing unnecessary latency for tag propagation and peer map updates. This replaces it with a 1ms micro-batch drain that processes operations as fast as they arrive while still coalescing concurrent writes. Throughput improved 2.5x.

**Files:** `node_store.go` (drainMicrobatch, revised processLoop)

### 8. `d802f381` hscontrol/state: store NodeIDs instead of NodeViews in peersByNode to eliminate GC overhead
**2 files, +215/-183**

Changed `peersByNode` from `map[NodeID][]NodeView` to `map[NodeID][]NodeID`. At 5000 nodes, the peer graph has ~25M entries. `NodeView` contains a pointer (forces GC to scan every entry), while `NodeID` is a `uint64` (GC skips it entirely). `ListPeers` materializes fresh `NodeView`s from `nodesByID` at read time. GC overhead dropped from 50% to 3%.

**Files:** `node_store.go` (Snapshot type, snapshotFromNodes, shallowSnapshot, incrementalSnapshot, refreshNodePeers, ListPeers), `node_store_test.go` (updated assertions for NodeID storage)

### 9. `a23ce2d1` hscontrol/policy: add pre-built node IP indexes for O(1) Username/Tag resolution
**2 files, +103/-5**

`Username.Resolve` and `Tag.Resolve` scanned all N nodes to build IP sets. This adds `buildNodeIPIndexes` which pre-builds `nodeIPsByUser` and `nodeIPsByTag` maps once per filter compilation cycle. Resolve methods do O(1) map lookups instead of O(N) scans.

**Files:** `policy.go` (buildNodeIPIndexes, integration into updateLocked/ensureFilterCompiled), `types.go` (nodeIPsByUser/nodeIPsByTag fields, Resolve fast paths)

### 10. `c04df66c` mapper/batcher: wake processing loop on new changes for prompt delivery
**2 files, +19/-0**

Adds a wake channel that signals the batcher's doWork loop to process pending changes immediately instead of waiting for the next tick interval. This ensures node additions and policy changes are delivered to connected clients without the full batch delay, preventing stale peer lists in fast registration scenarios. Also includes `UserProfiles` in `policyChangeResponse` so newly visible peers have displayable identity information.

**Files:** `mapper/batcher.go` (wake channel, immediate processing signal), `mapper/mapper.go` (WithUserProfiles in policyChangeResponse)

## Test coverage

- **Unit tests:** All `go test ./hscontrol/...` pass at every commit
- **Reachability tests:** 12 test functions covering equivalence, scale, symmetry, dynamic join/leave, tag changes, subnet routes, IP-based ACLs
- **IP-based ACL tests:** 16 scenarios covering direct IPs, CIDR ranges, IPv6, hosts entries, mixed identity+IP rules, subnet route overlap, dynamic node changes
- **Live container test:** 104/104 pass (50 containers, 10 users, 8 roles, 22 ACL rules)
- **Mega test:** 149/149 pass (100 containers, comprehensive ACL scenarios)

## Code changes (excluding tests and comments)

**+605 lines added, -62 removed = 543 net new lines of production code**

---

*This PR was developed with Claude (Anthropic) running overnight, performing iterative `pprof` profiling, optimization, and correctness verification against live headscale instances with thousands of nodes and brutal ACL policies.*

title: [Feature] Suggested Exit Node implementation
body:
### Use case

One of the biggest confusions our Headscale users have is "which exit node do I pick" - and some of the automation we are deploying for our installs is relatively painful if we have to manually specify exit nodes.

The Tailscale fix seems to be using suggestedExitNodes, which are basically an extension of the existing exitNodes structure.

Being able to use set --exit-nodes=auto:any (or other tags) creates a lot more flexibility and resiliency in clients.

### Description

This particular feature request has been around before, but I guess I'm coming at it from the perspective of... it's written?

I've written this as something that augments the current ACL json config with a new parameter "suggestedExitNodes" which takes an array of Aliases, and done all the bits.

Raising this as an issue here (and also mentioned on Discord) in the hopes that you see the maintenance burden of it low, and I can submit the PR for review and ultimately conclusion!

https://github.com/realworldtech/headscale/tree/feature/suggest-exit-nodes

### Contribution

- [x] I can write the design doc for this feature
- [x] I can contribute this feature

### How can it be implemented?

I've implemented this by augmenting the policy file to add compatibility for

```
"suggestExitNodes": ["exit-syd", "exit-mel"],
```

where `"exit-syd"` and `"exit-mel"` are Aliases (as already defined).

The Headscale response has been augmented to return the valid nodes.

  - I've tried to follow the protocol semantics correctly. suggest-exit-node only on peers, suggest-exit-node-ui on self node only. The peer loop at builder.go:268 explicitly sets HasAnySuggestions: false with a comment explaining why.
  - Empty set handling correct. HasSuggestedExitNodes() at policy.go:893 checks len(Ranges()) > 0 rather than just nil-checking — prevents showing suggestion UI when aliases resolve to zero IPs.
  - Nil safety. Both IsSuggestedExitNode and HasSuggestedExitNodes guard against nil pm and nil suggestExitNodeSet.
  - Uses Aliases type — supports hosts and CIDRs for specific node targeting, not just users/groups/tags. My first build used the AutoApprover struct to define these, but I realised pretty quickly I wanted to be able to choose specific nodes to be listed, so swapped back to Aliases.

title: [Bug] Exit node not visible / routes trafic with acl and autogroup:internet
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

Exit node is not visible when acl configured:
```
{
  "acls": [   
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["autogroup:internet:*"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Exit node is registered for user `gateway`, user is `user`. Without acl configured, node is visible and internet is reachable via node.

```
{
  "groups": {
    "group:gateway": ["gateway@"]
  },
  "acls": [
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["group:gateway:*"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["autogroup:internet:*"]
    }
  ]
}
```
With that acl, exit node becomes visible and ping-able, but internet is not reachable via exit node.

```
{
  "acls": [
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["group:gateway:*"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["autogroup:internet:*"]
    },
    {
      "action": "accept",
      "src": ["*"],
      "dst": ["0.0.0.0/0:*"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Only with allow of `0.0.0.0/0:*` internet via exit node becomes reachable.

### Expected Behavior

Exit node is visible and forwards trafic with documented allow rule:
```
{
  "action": "accept",
  "src": ["*"],
  "dst": ["autogroup:internet:*"]
}
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Setup headscale
2. Add exit node with user `gateway`
3. Add client with another user `user`
4. Check exit node reachability and internet via exit node
5. Configure ACL
6. Check again

### Environment

```markdown
- OS:Ubuntu 22.04
- Headscale version:v0.0.0-20260401131042-835db974b5cd
- Tailscale 1.82.4 on Android
- Tailscale 1.96.4 on Linux (Ubuntu)
```

### Runtime environment

- [x] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Root Cause
Two bugs in the policy compilation pipeline:
1. hscontrol/policy/v2/filter.go — autogroup:internet skipped entirely
compileNetPortRanges() had a continue for autogroup:internet with a comment
saying it is handled via AllowedIPs/exit node routing.

No FilterRule entries were generated for internet ranges
matcher.MatchesFromFilterRules() produced empty matchers
CanAccess() could not determine exit node visibility via DestsIsTheInternet()
Clients received an empty PacketFilter and dropped all internet-bound traffic locally

2. hscontrol/policy/policyutil/reduce.go — rules stripped from exit node's filter
Even if explicit internet CIDR rules existed, ReduceFilterRules() stripped them
from the exit node's PacketFilter because any CIDR overlapping 0.0.0.0/0
(an exit route) was unconditionally skipped:

With current fix, ACL works fine: https://github.com/max-mal/headscale/commit/061ba42bfe3f8b001309515bcefb38b9beb9df0c

title: [Bug] Tagged nodes' expiry reset from nil to zero-time on restart (incomplete #2862 fix)
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

Key expiry for [tagged](https://tailscale.com/docs/features/tags#key-expiry) devices is disabled by default.

After updating headscale to v0.28.0 and its introduction of tags, tagged nodes (registered via tag-only pre-auth keys) have their expiry reset from nil/unset to `0001-01-01 00:00:00` (Go zero-time) whenever tailscaled restarts or the node re-registers with Auth=nil.

e.g.:
Before restart:
  headplane-agent | tagged-devices | tag:headplane-agent | Expiration: N/A

After restart:
  headplane-agent | tagged-devices | tag:headplane-agent | Expiration: 0001-01-01 00:00:00

The node appears to continue to function (IsExpired() treats both nil and zero as "not expired"), but the expiry representation in the database and API changes from null to "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z", which affects downstream consumers (e.g. the headplane web-ui loses he "No expiry" badge because it checks `=== null`).

### Expected Behavior

Tagged nodes should preserve their nil expiry across tailscaled / headscale restarts.

The guard added in 3bd4ecd (fix for #2862) should also cover nodes with nil expiry.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a tag-only pre-auth key:
 headscale preauthkeys create --tags tag:test-agent

2. Register a node using that key (e.g. via tsnet or `tailscale up --authkey=...`)

3. Confirm the node's expiry is N/A (nil)
 
 4. Restart the node's tailscaled (or restart the headscale server)

5. Check the node's expiry again:
   ```
   headscale nodes list
   # Expiration: 0001-01-01 00:00:00
   ```

**Root cause trace:**

When tailscaled restarts with persisted state, it sends `RegisterRequest` with `Auth=nil` and `Expiry=time.Time{}` (zero). In `handleRegister()` (auth.go:67-80):

  ```go
  if req.Auth == nil {
      if node, ok := h.state.GetNodeByNodeKey(req.NodeKey); ok {
          // Guard added in 3bd4ecd for #2862:
          if req.Expiry.IsZero() && node.Expiry().Valid() && !node.IsExpired() {
              return nodeToRegisterResponse(node), nil
          }
          resp, err := h.handleLogout(node, req, machineKey)
  ```

For tagged nodes, `node.Expiry` is nil (intentionally set during creation at state.go:1316). `node.Expiry().Valid()` returns `false` for nil, so the guard fails and the request falls through to `handleLogout()`.

This changes Expiry from nil (proto field unset → CLI "N/A") to &time.Time{}
(proto field set to 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z → CLI "0001-01-01 00:00:00").

**Suggested fix:**

Change auth.go:76 from:
```go
if req.Expiry.IsZero() && node.Expiry().Valid() && !node.IsExpired() {
```
to:
```go
if req.Expiry.IsZero() && !node.IsExpired() {
```
`IsExpired()` (node.go:166-176) already returns false for both nil and zero-time expiry, so `node.Expiry().Valid()` is redundant. Removing it makes the guard cover all "not expired" nodes regardless of whether their expiry is nil or set.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: NixOS 25.11
- Headscale version: v0.28.0
- Tailscale version: 1.96.5 (host system); 1.88.2 (headplane-agent's internal tsnet)
- Number of nodes: 9 (1 tagged node affected: headplane-agent)
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

title: types, util: normalise hostnames from hostinfo instead of rejecting
body:
Fixes #3188.

Hostnames like `Joe's Mac mini` were dropped on registration (falling back to `invalid-<random>`) and then rejected on every MapRequest with `WRN Rejecting invalid hostname update from hostinfo`. Both paths now route through `util.NormaliseHostname`, which lowercases, strips characters outside `[a-z0-9-.]`, and truncates to 63 chars. The update is dropped only if the normalised value is still invalid (empty, or starts/ends with a dash). Existing `invalid-*` nodes self-heal on the next MapRequest.

### Also changes

Other previously-rejected inputs now succeed (all strictly more permissive, none silently corrupting):

| Input | After |
|---|---|
| `> 63 chars` | truncated to 63 |
| `test_node` | `testnode` |
| `Test@Host` | `testhost` |
| `server-北京-01` | `server--01` |

Still rejected: empty-after-strip (`🎉`, `@@@`), leading/trailing dash (`-test`, `test-`), too short.

### Left for follow-up

- `node.Hostname` is normalised but `node.Hostinfo.Hostname` keeps the raw client string. Peers get the normalised value via `tailcfg.Node.Name` and the raw via `Hostinfo` — matches Tailscale's model.
- `GivenName` has a DB unique index. Two nodes across different users normalising to the same label will race; the losing MapRequest fails with a constraint error and the client retries. Rare and self-limiting. Wiring `EnsureUniqueGivenName` into the update path would fix it, at the cost of added complexity — happy to do it if wanted.

body:
# Changes
Extend MatchFromFilterRule in hscontrol/policy/matcher/matcher.go to union CapGrant[].Dsts into the rule's destination set. Without this, a node that only receives capabilities (e.g. cap/relay, cap/relay-target) through a CapGrant is excluded from the grant issuer's peer map, which breaks peer relay on grant-only policies.
Close: https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/issues/2841  

# Peer Relay Test Method and Results
## Method
  - Objective: verify in a real environment that 100.64.0.2 and 100.64.0.4 can use peer relay through 100.64.0.3 when direct UDP connectivity is
    blocked.
  - Environment:
      - 100.64.0.2: headscale-server on 107.150.110.155
      - 100.64.0.3: relay node on 123.58.213.16 / 10-7-54-172
      - 100.64.0.4: client node on 10-60-53-172
      - Headscale was upgraded to the current branch build before testing.
  - Method:
      - Verified the baseline path was direct.
      - Added temporary iptables rules on both ends to block UDP 41641 between 0.2 and 0.4.
      - Configured the relay node to listen on 40000 and advertise 123.58.213.16:40000.
      - Re-tested with tailscale ping, tailscale status, and tailscale debug peer-relay-sessions.
      - Removed the temporary firewall rules after the test.

  - On the relay node, tailscale debug peer-relay-sessions showed an active session and increasing packet counts.
  - After removing the temporary blocks, the nodes returned to direct connectivity.

title: hscontrol: preserve nil expiry on tailscaled restart
body:
The guard added for #2862 in `handleRegister` checked
`node.Expiry().Valid()` before preserving node state on `Auth=nil +
Expiry=zero` registration requests. `Valid()` returns false when
`node.Expiry` is nil — the default for tagged nodes and for untagged
nodes registered against a preauth key with no default `node.expiry`
configured. Both fell through to `handleLogout`, which wrote
`&time.Time{}` (`0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`) over the original nil.

User-visible: `headscale nodes list` reports Expiration
`0001-01-01 00:00:00` after a tailscaled restart, the SQLite `expiry`
column holds the same value rather than NULL, and the CLI's Expired
column flips to `yes` (as #3262 reports).

`IsExpired()` already returns false for both nil and zero-time, so the
`Valid()` check was redundant. Drop it so all nil-expiry nodes are
covered by the same preservation path.

Tests cover tagged + untagged restart paths and check the fix at both
the NodeStore view and the raw `nodes.expiry` DB row.

Fixes #3170
Fixes #3262

title: [Bug] User owned re registration with zero expiry stores 0001-01-01 instead of NULL
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

When a user owned node registers or re registers with a pre auth key, if the client does not send an expiry AND `node.expiry` is configured as `0` (no default), the `nodes.expiry` column gets `0001-01-01 00:00:00` (Go zero time) instead of NULL.

### Expected Behavior

The column should be NULL, matching the behaviour for tagged nodes and the value consumers use to distinguish "no expiry" from "expired at year 1". The headplane "no expiry" badge is an example of a consumer that checks `=== null`.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Configure `node.expiry: 0` in headscale
2. `headscale preauthkeys create` for a user
3. Register a node with that key (client sends zero expiry by default)
4. `sqlite3 db.sqlite "SELECT id, hostname, expiry FROM nodes"` shows `0001-01-01 00:00:00` for that node
5. Expected: NULL

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Linux
- Headscale version: current master (after 6337a3db)
- Tailscale version: any
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [ ] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

Root cause is in `hscontrol/state/state.go`. Two sites build a non nil pointer to `regReq.Expiry` regardless of whether the value is zero time:

- Line 2132 (re registration with same MachineKey): `node.Expiry = &regReq.Expiry`
- Line 2231 (initial registration): `Expiry: &regReq.Expiry` passed to `createAndSaveNewNode`

Both were introduced in commit 6337a3db (fix for #3111). The `needsDefaultExpiry` guard at `state.go:1644` checks `.IsZero()` but only applies a default when `s.cfg.Node.Expiry > 0`, so when both the request and the config are zero the pointer to zero time survives to the database.

A regression test and fix are in an accompanying PR.

title: Nullable timestamps keep producing nil vs zero-time bugs — maybe fix at the type layer
body:
Same bug shows up on different code paths, roughly every release cycle: a `*time.Time` field on a node (usually `Expiry`) ends up pointing at a zero `time.Time` instead of being `nil`, and the DB row holds `0001-01-01 00:00:00` rather than NULL. Consumers that check for NULL (headplane's "no expiry" badge, for one) then see the wrong state.

### Why it keeps happening

- `time.Time` is a value type. `&regReq.Expiry` is a non-nil pointer whether the underlying time is zero or not.
- GORM persists that pointer as a zero-time row, not NULL.
- SQLite stores it as the string `0001-01-01 00:00:00`. Postgres stores it as a real timestamp at year 1. The symptom reads slightly differently per backend.
- There is no type-level guard. Every new call site that writes `node.Expiry = &something` has to remember to check `IsZero` first. We keep forgetting.
- Once it lands in the DB, `node.Expiry().Valid()` returns true (the pointer is non-nil), so most "has expiry" checks still pass. Only code comparing against SQL NULL / JSON `null` notices.

### Past instances

Bugs:
- #1711 — auth-key registration leaves expiry unset → `0001-01-01`
- #2087 — preauthkey registration in v0.23-beta2 → `0001-01-01`
- #2862 — MapRequest on oidc node resets expiry to `0001-01-01`
- #3111 — `oidc.expiry: 0` writes year 2318 (a different workaround for the same problem)
- #3170 — tagged node on tailscaled restart has its nil expiry overwritten with zero-time
- #3198 — user-owned re-registration with zero expiry → `0001-01-01`

Point fixes:
- #2875 — `Save` → `Updates` on MapRequest path
- #3122 — configurable default expiry (introduced the #3198 regression)
- #3113 — `oidc.expiry: 0` → nil instead of MaxDuration
- #3197 — preserve nil expiry on tagged restart
- #3199 — preserve nil expiry on user-owned re-registration

Related (not quite the same class but share the nil/zero/expired confusion):
- #1579 — preauth key expiration not set properly
- #1851 — expired node + NULL expiry reauth not working
- #3048 — expiration inconsistency on tag/personal conversion
- #3069 — tailscale client spinlocks on expiry=0 (workaround led to #3111)

### What a real fix might look like

Custom type on the Node struct:

```go
type Expiry time.Time

func (e Expiry) Value() (driver.Value, error) {
    if time.Time(e).IsZero() {
        return nil, nil
    }
    return time.Time(e), nil
}
func (e *Expiry) Scan(v any) error { /* NULL -> zero */ }
func (e Expiry) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) { /* zero -> null */ }
```

Field becomes `Expiry Expiry` (value, not pointer). Zero value persists as NULL, non-zero as a timestamp. `&time.Time{}` stops being representable — the whole class of bug is gone at the type. Same treatment would apply to `LastSeen` and any other nullable timestamp the codebase grows.

### Trade-offs

- Pro: kills the class. Every new call site inherits the fix.
- Pro: one mapping (zero ↔ NULL) across DB, JSON, and wire.
- Pro: backwards compatible on read — existing `0001-01-01` rows scan back to zero and serialise as `null` going forward.
- Con: touches ~20-40 call sites. NodeView accessor signature changes.
- Con: JSON API flips from `"expiry": "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"` to `"expiry": null`. That is the desired behaviour for headplane but is an API change and needs a CHANGELOG entry.
- Con: need to verify GORM `Select(...).Updates(...)` writes NULL when `Value()` returns nil. `sql.NullTime` relies on this so it should work, but worth a unit test on both sqlite and pg.
- Con: optional one-shot `UPDATE nodes SET expiry = NULL WHERE expiry < '1900-01-01'` for pre-existing bad rows. Self-heals on next registration otherwise.

### Status

Maybe. Point fixes have worked each time so far, but the cost is one user-visible bug per release cycle until someone files the next one. Dropping this here so the option is on the record and the links to prior instances don't get lost.

title: hscontrol: rewrite hostname logic to match Tailscale SaaS
body:
Two disagreeing ingest paths, three duplicate regexes, and a
random-suffix collision fallback that drifted from Tailscale SaaS.
Apostrophes, spaces, dots, `@`, and non-ASCII were alternately
rejected or stored as `invalid-<rand>`. Same class of bug has shipped
six times since 2022.

Replace custom sanitiser with `tailscale.com/util/dnsname.SanitizeHostname`
and `ValidLabel`. Collision bumping moves inside `NodeStore.PutNode` /
`UpdateNode` — serialised through the single writer goroutine, so
concurrent registrations cannot duplicate. Admin rename uses the new
`SetGivenName`, which rejects collisions with `ErrGivenNameTaken`
rather than silently rewriting.

Empty-input fallback is now the literal `node`. MagicDNS names change
on upgrade for nodes previously stored with a random suffix; raw
`Hostname` is unchanged.

If `dnsname` drifts from SaaS later, the client has drifted too — fix

The new HA tracking is losing track of secondary nodes as soon as all subnet routers are offline at once.

To be able to recover as soon as one of the subnet routers comes back online.

```json5
      ]

  ]
```

  ```
  sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
  ip link add dummy0 type dummy 
  ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev dummy0
  ```

None.

title: [Feature] Allow admin to allow single-character hostnames (hostname minimum length 1) in config
body:
### Use case

I run a self-hosted Headscale instance for my personal infrastructure. I have a node that I intentionally named `h`. When I recently rebuilt my Headscale instance, Headscale began rejecting this hostname with the following warning and automatically assigned a fallback name (`invalid-zwocy6k7`):

```
WRN Rejecting invalid hostname update from hostinfo
    error="hostname \"h\" is too short, must be at least 2 characters"
    current_hostname=invalid-zwocy6k7 node.id=5 rejected_hostname=h
```

This validation was introduced in [PR #2393](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/pull/2393) ([commit `89323b5`](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/commit/89323b5)), which added `if len(name) < 2 { return errors.New("name must be at least 2 characters long") }` inside `CheckForFQDNRules` in `hscontrol/util/dns.go` ([CHANGELOG 0.25.0 (2025-02-11)](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md#0250-2025-02-11)).

I believe this decision may have arisen from [ICANN SAC064 advisory](https://itp.cdn.icann.org/en/files/security-and-stability-advisory-committee-ssac-reports/sac-064-en.pdf). But my understanding is that blocking single-character hostnames at registration is a **misapplication** of this advisory. SAC064 §4.1.2 governs _DNS resolvers_, not hostname assignment. When a user is not connected to a tailnet, the responsibility of enforcing SAC064 §4.1.2 lies with **the operating system's DNS resolver, not Headscale.**

## Workaround

The current workaround is to stop the service and manually edit the SQLite database. This workaround requires knowledge outside the scope and documented usage of the `headscale` CLI and is therefore not a desirable user experience for self hosters.

### Example
```
$ docker compose down
$ docker run --rm -v app_headscale-data:/data \
    --user 1000:1000 alpine/sqlite /data/db.sqlite \
    "UPDATE nodes SET hostname='h', given_name='h' WHERE id=5;"
$ docker compose up -d
```


### Description

While a "safe default" of a minimum hostname length of 2 is perfectly reasonable, it should be overridable in the `config.yaml` by the admin:

```yaml
minimum_hostname_length: 1   # default: 2
```


Thank you for creating Headscale and for considering this request.

### Contribution

- [x] I can write the design doc for this feature
- [x] I can contribute this feature

### How can it be implemented?

I am willing to help contribute this config option if needed.
